papers.title: Learning from Failure Through Game Testing Feedback in Virtual Collaborative Design
papers.authors: Shulong Yan, Codesign Education, Yu Xia
papers.abstract: This study investigates how learning from failure can be supported through game design feedback activities in a virtual collaborative environment. Through analyzing video recordings of three checkpoint sessions in a two-week virtual game design camp with nine youth participants (ages 8-13), we identified six feedback styles and examined how designers responded to feedback. Our findings reveal that game design feedback in virtual environments transcends traditional linear relationships, forming a complex discursive relationship among testers, designers, and game artifacts. Screen sharing emerged as a crucial boundary object, facilitating communication and transforming traditional critique sessions into collaborative learning experiences. Facilitators played vital roles by modeling playfulness, vulnerability, and productive failure responses. The study demonstrates that successful virtual design feedback requires thoughtfully curated environments that balance structured facilitation with playful engagement. These findings have implications for design education in virtual settings and suggest new approaches for supporting learning from failure in collaborative contexts.

papers.title: Generative Failure: Learning Design in Programming with Generative
papers.authors: Hideki KONDO, Sayaka TOHYAMA, Shuntaro ISERI, Masaaki Ishii
papers.abstract: This study proposes the Generative Failure Method (GFM) to address challenges in applying Productive Failure to novice programming. Beginners often struggle with syntax errors, rarely compare diverse solutions, and lack tasks aligned with interests. Leveraging large language models (LLMs), GFM helps novices overcome initial barriers, adapt project goals, and incrementally cultivate open-ended exploration. Rather than imposing open-ended tasks, GFM expands problem contexts as learners progress. A pilot study found that LLM support enabled learners to produce functional applications, engage in iterative trial-and-error, and reframe “failure” as a constructive resource for learning.

papers.title: Cognitive Analysis of Composite Instructional Designs: New Directions for Research on Problem-Solving Prior to
papers.abstract: In problem-solving prior to instruction (PS -I), an initial problem -solving phase is followed by an explicit instruction phase. Research on PS -I designs has produced conflicting results that  cannot be explained by the learning mechanisms discussed so far in  this line of research. The present paper applies a recently developed framework, aimed at – more generally – analyzing composite instructional designs (CID; i.e., designs that include multiple instructional phases) to PS -I research. The CID framework supports an understanding of PS-I effects by attending to the effects on intermediate knowledge (i.e., the knowledge state after the initial problem -solving phase ) and discussing how this intermediate knowledge  affects the learning processes that occur during subsequent explicit instruction. The analysis with CID also highlights that experimental variations of the instructional design (e.g., comparing PS-I with I- PS) often affect multiple learning processes  and, thus, demonstrates the need for alternative research strategies when investigating the learning mechanisms of PS-I. Problem-solving prior to instruction (PS-I) Problem-solving prior to instruction (PS-I) is an instructional design  in which students are first asked to solve a problem targeting a yet unknown concept (often implemented in a collaborative setting; Brand et al., 2023; Mazziotti et al., 2019) before receiving instructional explanations about the underlying concept and the canonical problem solution (Kapur & Bielaczyc, 2012) . Several studies have found positive effects of PS -I compared to I-PS (i.e., explicit instruction prior to problem solving) on the acquisition of conceptual knowledge (for overviews see Loibl et al., 2017; Sinha & Kapur, 2021). However, the evidence from studies that compare the effects of variants of the instructional design on learning outcomes is not yet conclusive: Sometimes PS -I is more effective than I -PS, sometimes it is not (Loibl et al., 2017; Sinha & Kapur, 2021). Sometimes watching someone else solve a problem (so -called vicarious problem solving) prior to explicit instruction is as effective as own problem solving, sometimes it is not (e.g., Hartmann et al., 2022 vs. Kapur, 2014). Sometimes studying worked solutions prior to explicit instruction is more, sometimes less effective than problem solving (e.g., Glogger-Frey et al., 2015 vs. 2017). In a theoretical review, Loibl et al. (2017) identified three mechanisms that may explain the PS-I effect: 1) In the problem-solving phase, students activate their prior knowledge when generating solution ideas. 2) As they usually do not come up with a canonical solution, they may become aware of their knowledge gaps. 3) This awareness, in turn, may help students to focus on the relevant features when they receive instructional explanations. While these assumed mechanisms are grounded in the general literature on learning and instruction, they have not been studied in isolation in the context of PS -I. Thus, it is unclear whether and at to what extend each of these mechanisms actually contributes to the PS-I effect. A key feature of PS -I is that it comprises two  phases with different learning goals and different pedagogical approaches. Such composite designs are frequent in instruction – in research as well as in practice (Kunter, 2005; Prediger et al., 2021; Stigler et al., 1999). In order to resolve the conflicting findings in PS -I research presented above, it seems relevant to better understand the underlying mechanisms resulting from the relationship between the two phases. An appropriate means to do so is a recently developed framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs (CID) (Loibl et al., subm.) which allows us to look beyond the instructional design level. Framework for cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs (CID) Research on PS -I usually focuses on the level of instructional design by comparing PS -I with I-PS or different variants of PS-I and investigating the effect of these experimental variations on learning outcomes (Loibl et al., 2017; Sinha & Kapur, 2021). Only few studies investigate the learning processes in PS -I, mostly by relying on data on the quality, quantity, and diversity of students’ solutions (e.g., Kapur & Bielazyc, 2012; Loibl & Rummel, 2014a). However, a better understanding of the learning processes at play would be essential to provide explanations for the effects on learning outcomes . Koedinger et al. (2012) proposed the so-called Knowledge- Learning-Instruction (KLI) framework. One of the intentions of the authors was to relate elements at the three levels of knowledge components, learning processes , and instructional design to provide a better understanding of how instructional design elements stimulate learning processes and result in better learning outcomes. Building on this rationale, our recently developed framework for conducting cognitive analyses of composite instructional designs (CID; Loibl et al., subm.) links the three levels – (K) knowledge components, (L) learning processes, and (I) instructional design – across multiple phases (see Figure 1; Loibl et al., subm.). Analyses which apply the CID framework highlight that changing the instructional design of the first phase (I 1) changes the learning processes in this phase (L 1), resulting in different intermediate knowledge (K 1) (i.e., the knowledge state after the first phase, in PS-I after the initial problem-solving phase). This intermediate knowledge, in turn, is the starting point for the subsequent phase. As the learning processes in the subsequent phase (L 2) are not only affected by the instructional design of the second phase (I 2), but also build on the knowledge resulting from the first phase  (K1), the learning processes (L2) necessarily unfold differently  after different instructional designs of the first phase. Figure 1 The CID framework (Loibl et al., subm.) integrates the phases of a composite instructional design and the three levels – knowledge, learning, and instruction. The white boxes specify the elements of the framework for the PS-I condition of the first example below (Copyright Figure: K. Loibl & T. Leuders) The CID framework serves as a schema for specifying the underlying theoretical assumptions about the learning mechanisms of composite instructional designs such as PS -I. We suggest that research on the learning mechanisms underlying PS-I could benefit from incorporating the following two steps: (1) specifying the elements of the CID framework for the proposed PS-I design, and (2) analyzing (theoretically and empirically) the changes that result at all three levels when implementing variations of  the PS-I design. By analy zing the effects of the design of the problem -solving phase (I1) and the corresponding problem -solving processes (L 1) on intermediate knowledge (K 1) and how this intermediate knowledge alters the learning processes (L 2) initiated during the subsequent explicit instruction (I2), we can gain a better understanding of the learning mechanisms that make PS-I conducive for learning. We suggest that a systematic reason for the conflicting results found in previous research (e.g., Glogger-Frey et al., 2015 vs. 2017; Hartmann et al., 2022 vs. Kapur, 2014) lies in the interdependence of the learning mechanisms across the different phases, which could be highlighted by applying the CID framework. Applying the CID framework to PS-I research A first example for the application of CID to PS -I designs refers to research that compares two types of first phases: solving the problem in a PS-I condition (cf. specification in the white boxes of Figure 1) with working through a worked solution to the same problem in a worked-solution condition (WS-I) (Glogger-Frey et al., 2015, 2017). This instructional variation can alter the depth of knowledge acquired during the first phase, which in turn also affects the learning processes in the second phase. Glogger-Frey and colleagues conducted two studies using this design. The only difference between the two studies consisted in the duration of the initial phase. Students in the first study (Glogger -Frey et al., 2015) went through one problem ( either solving the problem or working through a worked solution depending on the condition), whereas students in the second study (Glogger -Frey et al., 2017) went through two problems during the initial learning phase (also both conditions). In the first study, students in the problem -solving condition (I 1) likely generate d solutions that included relevant and irrelevant surface features (L1), resulting in unstructured intermediate knowledge , including relevant and surface features (K1). In contrast, students in the worked-solution condition encoded only relevant features. During the subsequent explicit instruction (I 2), all students encoded the given explanations (L2). Students in the problem -solving condition also had to sort irrelevant surface features from relevant features (L2), whereas students in the worked- solution condition did not. Not surprisingly, students in the worked -solution condition outperformed their counterparts on the post -test (K2). In the second study, students in the problem -solving condition could acquire negative knowledge (Oser et al., 1999) about the irrelevance of surface features (K 1) by working through two problems (L1). In this case, the problem-solving condition outperformed the worked solution condition at posttest (K2). Thus, the key to explaining the seemingly inconsistent results reported by Glogger -Frey and colleagues (2015 vs. 2017) lies in the differences in the quality of the intermediate knowledge influenced by the type and the duration of the first phase: Only sufficiently comprehensive and structured  intermediate knowledge provides fertile ground for learning from subsequent instruction. As a second example for the application of the CID framework on PS-I designs, we discuss research that switches the sequence of problem solving and explicit instruction (PS-I vs. I-PS), which has been a paradigm in research on PS-I (Sinha & Kapur, 2021; Loibl et al., 2017). Studies comparing PS-I and I-PS have been conducted in cognitive domains (e.g., on the concept of variance, Kapur, 2012; Loibl & Rummel, 2014b) as well as in motor learning (javelin throwing, Loibl & Leukel, 2023) with similar beneficial effects of PS -I. At the instructional design level, comparing PS-I and I-PS seems to be a fair comparison to test the effect of the sequence, at least when using the same materials in both conditions (Loibl & Rummel, 2014b; Loibl et al., 2020) . However, when explicitly considering the level of learning processes, it becomes clear that changing the instructional sequence (PS-I vs. I-PS) has multiple effects: Generating own solution attempts in an initial problem-solving phase allows for forming negative knowledge  (i.e., knowledge about what does not work)  and for encoding own examples (intermediate knowledge, K1). This intermediate knowledge (K1) then can be linked to the processed explanations in the second phase (L 2). This learning process is not present when the explanations are given in the first phase. Additionally, the switching of instructional types also completely changes the processes in the problem -solving phase: In PS-I, the learning processes in the problem-solving phase are activating prior knowledge and identifying knowledge gaps , while generating own solution attempts  (L1). Together, these processes promote negative knowledge and encoded examples as early forms of conceptual knowledge (K 1). In I-PS, the learning processes in the problem-solving phase, which comes second here, are more about practicing the application of the procedure that was introduced in the initial explicit instruction phase (L 2). This learning process does not affect conceptual knowledge but rather only strengthens procedural knowledge (K2). Thus, by changing the order of the instructional phases, more than one learning mechanism is altered, as the intermediate knowledge affects the learning processes in the second learning phase in both implemented orders . Therefore, while unconfounded at the instructional design level, any assumptions on the specific mechanisms at work are empirically highly confounded at the learning process level. Conclusions Based on our analyses of PS -I research using the CID framework, we could demonstrate that intermediate knowledge plays a significant role in understanding the underlying mechanisms  of PS-I, as it influences the learning processes in the second phase. Moreover, by specifying all three levels (knowledge components, learning processes, and instructional design)  across the two phases for the example studies (for more detailed analyses, also beyond PS-I research, see Loibl et al. subm.), we have demonstrated that modifying the instructional design can have an effect on various mechanisms at the other two levels. Consequently, specifying all three levels can potentially explain previous conflicting results. In addition, the CID analyses show that understanding individual mechanisms requires research strategies that not only carefully control the instructional design but also consider the resulting alterations in learning processes and knowledge across all implemented conditions. papers.title: Learning From Errors and Worked Examples to Address Common Misunderstandings in Linear Functions Knowledge
papers.abstract: A series of studies were conducted to explore designs for instructional interventions, including worked examples and learning from errors, that can address misunderstandings in linear functions  (LF) knowledge of college students. Study 1 focused on identifying and modeling errors that students most commonly make during the essential conceptual and procedural components of the problem-solving process for different types of LF items. Study 2 then addressed common errors by testing the efficacy of di fferent forms of worked example (WE) presentation. Findings from Study 2 led to changes in the design of the WE  which were then tested in Study 3. Overall, the findings support the importance of tailoring learning interventions to the learner. Instructional interventions using WE and learning from errors can be tailored to address common misunderstandings for important mathematical topics such as LF. Major issues One topic that college students struggle with and could benefit from instructional intervention is linear functions (LF). Reasoning with and about LF is considered essential knowledge for college and career readiness (e.g., Conley et al., 2011). Understanding essentials of linear algebra requires cognitive flexibility, such as moving between tabular, algebraic, graphic, and semantic representations, as well as moving between abstract, algebraic, and geometric languages, sometimes all in one task (Mainali, 2 021). Evidence suggests that college students experience considerable difficulty solving even simple LF problems (Mielicki & Wiley, 2016). The focus of Study 1 was to explore and model common types of errors that students make in these types of problems that lead to pervasive difficulty. Observations about the nature of the errors led to the design and development of an instructional intervention comprising worked examples and error-processing tasks. Worked example (WE) presentation as an instructional intervention has proven to be an effective learning tool. To increase this benefit, WE can be paired with error-processing tasks (e.g., Booth et al., 2013). The focus of Study 2 explored what specific design of WE and error -processing tasks is most beneficial for which learners. There were two major observations from Study 2. While presenting WE for LF algebra problems with and without error -related processing tasks did result in significantly higher performance in comparison to only solving problems, exposure to this intervention was not equally beneficial for all learners. The disparity in benefit from these interventions require d further exploration to 1) explain the  disparity in outcomes, and 2) augment the current intervention design to address this issue. This was the focus of Study 3. Literature on learning from errors indicates that favorable prior knowledge of the domain is essential to meaningfully engaging with error processing tasks (e.g., Kapur, 2016). As such, students may require support to guide them through meaningfully processing erroneous examples. Thus, there may be additional conditions beyond those established in the current literature that inform the effectiveness of WE with errors as an instructional intervention. Study 3 tested the efficacy of an augmented design of the WE with error -processing tasks tha t promote the retrieval of relevant prior knowledge to support error processing for those who otherwise have difficulty doing so. The following sections expand on the theory, methods, results, and implications of Stud ies 1, 2, and 3. Theoretical and methodological approach(es) pursued: Study 1 Study 1 was conducted to understand the nature of college students’ misunderstandings in the solution of LF problems. The study explored solution accuracy on LF problems presented in different contexts, common error types, and consideration of major conceptual and procedural errors exhibited by students. This included examining the cognitive underpinnings of the solution process with a focus on the students’ schem atic knowledge for representation of the given problem types. This was done by qualitative coding of students’ solutions to description, graph, and table LF problems with a particular focus on errors to provide insight into the cognitive underpinnings of misunderstandings that students typically have in this knowledge domain. In Study 1, data were collected from 151 college students enrolled in an introductory psychology class at a U.S. research intensive public university with a diverse student population. Students were given 21 total LF problems, 7 graph, 7 table, and 7 description items, in an open -response format which required subjects to 971 demons trate the actions they take in generating a solution. Responses were scored based on accuracy, and erroneous responses were further analyzed based on  the nature of the error as mapped to a specific discrepancy in LF knowledge. Major findings, conclusions, implications: Study 1 Accuracy analyses showed that overall performance was highest on description problems (M = 5.46, SD = 1.34) and lowest on graph ( M = 3.08, SD = 2.40) and table ( M = 3.85, SD = 2.66) problems. Considering these performance levels, comprehensive error analyses focused on responses to Table and Graph problems. Study 1 data suggest that there are common conceptual  and procedural errors that students consistently make while solving these problems. Students demonstrated a tendency to make rational, rule-based errors that are conditional on the format in which the problem information is presented. The errors observed in both problem types demonstrate that students commonly conceptualize tables and graphs as a compilation of individual points, instead of understanding that those points make up a conceptual entity (Kaput, 2018). Thus, it seems that the surface-structural characteristics of these problems contribute to the erroneous solutions of these types of LF problems. Theoretical and methodological approach(es) pursued: Study 2 In mathematics learning, a common root of most errors is an overgeneralization of rules, meaning that the conditions of the rules were encoded in an overly general way and as such apply to more situations than is correct or appropriate. Therefore, they are  activated and applied in situations incorrectly. Thus, correcting the error generally relies on the specialization of the target knowledge (Ohlsson, 1996). The specialization hypothesis states that to correct errors caused by overly generalized rules, more information about the respective task environments needs to be integrated into the rules. One common approach to achieve this using error learning is by integrating error-processing tasks in WE.  Tasks that involve detecting and correcting errors have been shown to benefit learning because they promote adaptive conceptual thinking (Beege et al., 2021; Kapur, 2016). Study 2 focused on testing the learning benefits of WE paired with different error -processing tasks. 278 total subjects were presented with a pretest of basic LF knowledge, then the instructional materials which comprised the intervention, followed by a LF post -test serving as a learning outcome measure. The intervention presented 2 of either table or graph LF problems that were correctly worked out , t hen 5 of one of the three experimental variations of the same problem type: LF problems that are: (1) worked-out solutions requiring error detection, (2) worked-out solutions that indicated an error, or (3) worked -out solutions to the problems with no error. The errors exemplified in the erroneous WE were the most common of the error types observed in Study 1 for each problem type. Major findings, conclusions, implications: Study 2 Visualization of posttest data indicated non -normal distributions for all groups, and a Shapiro- Wilk test of normality indicated that the data was non -normal (W = 0.79, p < .001). For all groups most scores fall near the extremes at 0 and 7 as opposed to centering around the respective scale mean, as observed in Study 1. This suggests that intervention exposure shifted the pattern of student performance for these problems such that they are answering most or all the questions either correctly or incorrectly regardless of the condition mean. Posttest performance was compared to a baseline performance estimate established by the normative results obtained in Study 1 for those same problems. For both graph and table problem groups all three intervention conditions led to improved performance compared to the Study 1 baseline estimate, but the Error Indicated (Graph: U = 5081, p < .001; Table: U = 3867, p = 0.05) and No Error (Graph: U = 4276, p < .001; Table: U = 4525.5, p = 0.03) groups showed significant differences in performance. The Error Detection groups did not show performance differences relative to the Study 1 baseline estimate (Graph: U = 3981.5, p = 0.30; Table: U = 4004, p = 0.27). However, for those whose misunderstanding was not directly addressed in the intervention, relevant prior knowledge was not successfully activated, so, they did not map the focal conceptual features of the solution in the example to their knowledge of LF. As a result, those students answered most or all the posttest questions incorrectly. This suggests that interventions with error- processing tasks may only be beneficial if the presented errors reflect the specific misunderstandings that students have. Theoretical and methodological approach(es) pursued: Study 3 Study 2 findings emphasize the role that prior knowledge plays in the learning process. The learners who were able to benefit from the intervention demonstrated evidence of learning benefits as observed in the improvement 972 of pe rformance on the posttest. The intervention was able to facilitate meaningful learning processes when the error in their knowledge was made salient to them in the WE and revision of the faulty knowledge was enabled through error-processing tasks. As useful and beneficial erroneous WE may be, certain learners are not able to benefit from this intervention design because the current intervention designs do not support learning in those who have low prior knowledge of the topic. Research shows that favorable prior knowledge of the domain is essential to meaningfully engaging with error processing tasks (e.g. , Zhang & Fiorella, 2023). Error detection and correction requires domain-specific declarative and practical knowledge (Kapur, 2016), and a common misunderstanding students seem to have is overly generalized domain knowledge structures. As such, students may require support to guide them through meaningfully processing erroneous examples, with the goal of specialization of the target knowledge. One strategy in improving the current design of this intervention could be through the integration of conceptually-relevant prerequisite knowledge analogs. Research by Sidney and Alibali (2015) and Leech et al., (2008) has shown the benefit of exposure to such analogs in learning new concepts because it activates relevant conceptual prior knowledge before instruction to facilitate learning. This is because presenting structurally similar analogs can facilitate the retrieval of prior conceptual knowledge needed to process subsequent information. The nature of the errors observed in Study 1 and 2 indicated that subsequent instruction should focus on specialization of LF knowledge. Thus, structural analogs of prerequisite LF knowledge could be designed in a way that presents what students do know about tables and graphs and guide them to construct accurate representations of them in the context of LF. To this end, the analogs presented in the intervention in Study 3 guided subjects in reconceptualizing tables and graphs through mapping the individua l points either from a table to a graph or from a graph to a table. Guiding them through forming the graph or table themselves makes it salient that these points can be assembled to form an entity which  can be extracted to form an algebraic expression to represents each entity. Study 3 included 234 subjects who were first presented with the same pretest as Study 2, then the structural analogs were presented before one of three intervention conditions, 1) error detection, 2) error indicated, or 3) no worked example. The condition with no worked example, which differs from Study 2, test ed whether exposure to the analog itself could lead to learning benefits. Lastly, all groups were presented with the same posttest as Study 2. Major findings, conclusions, implications: Study 3 Visualization of posttest data again revealed non -normal distributions for all groups. A Shapiro- Wilk test of normality indicated that the data were non- normal (W = 0.61, p < .001). For all groups the data reflected a negatively skewed distribution as opposed to an even distribution between the extremes 0 and 7 as observed in Study 2. This suggests that the change in the intervention has caused a shift in the pattern of student performance for these problems, such that most subjects are now solving posttest problems correctly. To test the efficacy of the addition of structural analogs to the intervention, posttest performance after intervention exposure was compared to a baseline performance estimate established by the normative results obtained in Study 2 for those same problems. For both graph and table problem groups all three intervention conditions led to improved performance compared to performance in Study 2, but the Error Indicated groups (Graph: U = 968.5, p = .01; Table: U = 1316, p = 0.00) and Error Detection in Table group (U = 837.5, p = 0.00) showed statistically significant differences in performance. The Error Detection Graph group (U = 1215.5, p = 0.21), as well as both groups in the No Example condition, which was compared to the Study 1 baseline performance to establish the role of only analog presentation, did not show significant performance differences relative to Study 2 performance (Graph: U = 3109.5, p = .10; Table: U = 3321.5, p = 0.130). Findings from Study 3 showed a significant improvement in performance for those who were exposed to erroneous WE that were paired with structural analogs that specifically addressed common misunderstandings that students had. This indicates that the addition of the analogs facilitated the processes that were needed for certain students to benefit from the WE and error processing tasks. Moreover, we found that presenting the analogs on their own to students did not lead to learning benefits, further indicating that the fundamental aspect of this intervention is pairing the analog with the erroneous WE. Potential significance of the work This series of studies brought to light several findings that ultimately led to the design of an effective intervention. Study 1 established the glaring need for an intervention for LF topic knowledge. Findings suggested that learning from WE with and without different error -processing tasks could be a potentially useful intervention given the nature of the errors observed, which was the focus of Study 2. Findings from Study 2 indicated differential levels 973 of per formance improvement relative to the different intervention designs. This was addressed in Study 3 in which erroneous WE were paired with analogs that focused on facilitating the construction of accurate representations of graphs and tables. Ultimately, this led to an overall increase in learning benefits indicating that the discrepancy between the mental representations that students construct and the problem situation, which has caused low performance in these problems, can be addressed by pairing WE error-processing tasks with analogs. Findings from these studies point to significant weaknesses in how students were previously instructed, what they ultimately learned about LF, and ultimately, their relative inability to engage in solving LF problems of the type often found in multiple areas of higher education study. Furthermore, results from the intervention studies take into account that typical student misunderstandings have implications for how students could be instructed when they learn algebra earlier in their education, as well as the importance of diagnostic assessment procedures to help detect and correct common misunderstandings that could be used to select effective instructional adaptations for individual students. papers.title: Sowing Seeds for Applying Productive Failure to Reading: Pre-Reading Questions Alone are Not Enough to Reap the Benefits
papers.authors: Zack Carpenter, Jennifer Cromley, Martin Van Boekel
papers.abstract: There is no know n work mapping Productive Failure  (PF)—a popular pedagogical design within the Learning Sciences—to reading. Therefore, through a secondary data analysis of students reading several expository biology excerpts, the current work attempts to bridge PF and reading. One group of students answered questions before reading the passages, while the other group did not. The results revealed that pre -reading questions had no effect on the acquisition of causal language, but the different passages did affect causal language pickup. Productive failure and prereading questions Evidence suggests that embracing failure in educational settings promotes learning (Williams-Pierce et al., 2021), with Productive Failure (PF) being one effective learning design (Sinha & Kapur, 2021). PF studies demonstrate enhanced learning, particularly in STEM (Sinha & Kapur, 2021), but there's limited exploration in non -STEM areas despite calls for such research (Loibl et al., 2017). Our focus  here is on applying PF to reading through examining the impact of prereading questions on understanding causa l language pickup (Cromley et al., 2020). While there's no direct link between PF and reading, we argue prereading questions are one bridge  (Lewis & Mensink, 2012). Bringing together PF and reading offers a generative opportunity for the Learning Sciences, especially because there are apparent shared mechanisms. Productive Failure involves two phases: (1) a problem- solving phase where students generate solutions to a complex problem they don't know how to solve, leading to initial failure, and (2) a direct instruction phase introducing the canonical  solution (Sinha & Kapur, 2021). It incorporates design considerations across the activity, participation structures, and social surround. Students in PF activities often outperform those receiving instruction first, and the mechanisms said to contribute to PF's effectiveness include activating prior knowledge, highlighting critical conceptual features, explaining and elaborating on concepts, and organizing critical features into concepts (Sinha & Kapur, 2021). Pre-reading questions influence reading processes, including the identification of causal language crucial for forming a comprehensive situation model (Cromley et al., 2020). The situation model is a mental construct of the text that extends beyond the comprehension of individual words and sentences. Considering some mechanisms in the context of Productive Failure (PF), this research  investigates how prereading questions influence the identification of causal language.  Firstly, answering questions before reading a text can activate pertinent prior knowledge about a topic (Alemi & Ebadi, 2010). We predict that this activation will prompt readers to notice relevant causal language necessary to answer the questions while they are reading the text. Secondly, we anticipate that readers will be drawn to pre-reading related text elements , thereby increasing the likelihood of identifying the causal language within the text (Lewis & Mensink, 2012) . With these two mechanistic predictions in mind, we pose the following research question: Do prereading questions lead to greater identification of causal language during the reading process?

papers.title: Learning in Productive Failure
papers.abstract: In Productive Failure (PF), students are prepared for subsequent  instruction by activating prior knowledge and becoming aware of own knowledge gaps when generating solution attempts to an unknown problem. Intermediate knowledge after solution generation likely affords the subsequent integration of new knowledge, but has only seldom been assessed in composite instructional designs such as PF. We investigated how the learning processes and (intermediate) knowledge in PF vary when manipulating the PF tasks’ goal formulations (learning vs. problem -solving goals). As hypothesized, learning goals led to higher gap awareness prior to instruction, higher closing of gaps after instruction as well as better learning outcomes compared to the problem -solving goals. Moreover, broad knowledge activation during the first learning phase correlated with the intermediate knowledge state. Contrary to our hypotheses, knowledge activation and gap awareness did not mediate the learning outcomes.

papers.title: Community, Creativity, and Identity in Generative Role-Play Based Learning
papers.authors: Rich Paul Cooper, Mahjabin Chowdury, Jonan Phillip Donaldson, Adam Pawson
papers.abstract: This study examines learner experiences in generative role- playing game -based learning implemented in a university science fiction literature course. Through complex systems thematic network analysis of student reflections, we investigated how principles f rom learning theories manifested in the game -based learning experience. Analysis revealed five distinct clusters of principles, with constructionist elements showing the highest network centrality. The findings suggest that game creation and world- building serve as powerful tools for literary education, with students navigating multiple identities—both real and fictional—throughout the course. The study identified an important prerequisite for engagement: students must either leverage existing gamer identit ies or develop new ones before fully engaging in the creative process. This research contributes to understanding how game -based learning can facilitate transformative learning experiences in literature courses, while highlighting the need for better integration of productive failure and tinkering principles in future design iterations.

papers.title: Developing Approaches to Racial Justice in the Learning Sciences
papers.authors: Bella Afra Boateng, Joe Curnow, Anny Chen, Abolitionist Futures Collective, Rachel Folger, Stephanie T. Jones, Sarah Priscilla Lee, Natalie Araujo Melo, Raesheena Kennedy, KIPP Columbus, Talia Leibovitz, Ashieda McKoy, Joseph L. Polman, Beatriz Salazar, Trang C. Tran
papers.abstract: In this symposium, we build on the legacies and ongoing work of scholars across fields who have made room for research and teaching involving literacies and practices of racial justice. In recent years, we have seen even deeper engagement with these conversations within the learning sciences, as the shift toward addressing the political and ethical dimensions of learning has come into focus. Through this structured poster session, we expand theoretical underpinnings and attend to the ways that emerging scholars from different areas of the learning sciences are taking up the mantle. What does racial justice look like in the learning sciences? What does it look like, feel like, and sound like to advance racial justice in the learning sciences? What has racial justice meant? For whom? And, to what end? In this symposium, we build on the legacies and ongoing work of scholars across fields who have made room for research and teaching involving literacies and practices of racial justice. The session explores what it means to advance racial justice globally in this era, where the backlash against movements for racial repair and remediation has grown. Hostility against racial justice movements is evident in the systematic censorship of speech in education, increases in xenophobic policies, and escalating incidents of racialized violence interpersonally and by various state apparatuses. Moments like these require scholars of learning to mobilize our teaching, research, and service to advance justice projects (Politics of Learning Writing Collective, 2017), and to think carefully about the role of learning in addressing historicized power relations (Esmonde & Booker, 2017). However, racial justice has largely remained on the periphery of learning sciences work, and so in this moment of racialized backlash, we  look to scholarship and praxis from racial justice movements and literature to anchor our collective work in support of racial justice within the learning sciences. Our structured poster session invites participants to reflect on diverse racial justice traditions and interrogate if and how these theoretical keystones might generate new insights into learning toward justice. Since the learning sciences’ founding, some learning scientists have always been attentive to relations of power embedded in historicity and identity. From the earliest days, our predecessors have compellingly argued that racialization, ethnicity, class, and culture are key facets of learning ecologies that must be addressed analytically (Lee 1995; Rogoff, 1981; Gutierrez 1992, Nasir, 2002; Nasir & Hand, 2006; Rose 2001, Saxe, 1984). These foundations have created a fertile ground for further engagement across educational research fields that centrally address racialization, including critical race theory in education (e.g., Ladson -Billings & Tate, 1995), ethnic 2381 studies (e.g., Cammarota, 2016; de los Rios, et al., 2015), critical Indigenous pedagogies (e.g., Tachine & Nicolazzo, 2020), decolonial studies (e.g., Bajaj, 2022; Battiste, 2002; Zavala, 2016), and other specialized fields. In recent years, we have seen even deeper engagement with these conversations within the learning sciences, as the shift toward addressing the political and ethical dimensions of learning has come into focus (Esmonde & Booker, 2017). This growing scholarship emphasizes that learning is cultural  and embedded within current systems of injustice and that all conceptualizations of learning are connected to political systems (Madkins & McKinney de Royston, 2019). Within the learning sciences, attention to racial-ideological tensions in teaching and learning is generating important directions for learning scholarship. For instance, Philip (2011) and  Sengupta- Irving et al. (2021) reveal a need for racial literacy development, arguing that these skills are both distinctive from other disciplinary learning and needed in the context of deep, historical racial injustice. Another key focus of scholarship observes how learners imagine possibilities for racial justice through organizing and design (e.g., Pham & Philip, 2021; Arada et al., 2023). These approaches draw our collective attention to how learning and racial justice can and should be imbricated in our field to theorize learning in situ, where racial injustice is hegemonic and where calls to action from communities, movements, educators, and young people have urged us to take substantive action to remake racial relations of power. As we work to build racial justice scholarship in the learning sciences, we remain attentive to the relations, power, and processes that shape learning. We recognize that many scholars actively make space for discussions of race and racial justice within ICLS itself (Curnow, 2021; Marin et al., 2022; Jones et al., 2023; Rodgers, 2023; Shaw et al., 2023; Tzou et al., 2023; Leibovitz et al., 2024), contribute to ongoing dialogue about how we do this work, what counts as knowledge, and make way for alternative ways of being that are de-colonial, non-extractive, and meaningfully anti-racist. We affirm that such methodological considerations about how, why, for, and with whom we do research, are critical for advancing and understanding approaches to racial justice. As evidenced by the overlaps in our thinking, learning is inherently reflexive, community -centered, intersectional, and taking action toward an otherwise (Tachine & Nicolazzo, 2023). In this structured poster session, we take up critical perspectives, expand theoretical underpinnings to include new-to-the-field approaches to theorizing race, racialization, and racial justice, and attend to the ways that emerging scholars from different areas of the learning sciences are taking up the mantle. Collectively, we position our work within the learning sciences’ long -standing engagement with diversity and equity goals while actively integrating theoretical contributions from the broader fields of education, critical ethnic studies, Black studies, and other fields attuned to racial justice. We aim to offer a generative space to push ourselves and participants to make a deeper commitment to understanding racial relations of power across space, place, time, and condition, and centering these concerns in our design, theorization, and knowledge mobilization. Synergies within our work emphasize that racial justice is ultimately a relational endeavor. Through collective designs that center minoritized ways of knowing and being and pay attention to relations as both process and product (Bang & Vossoughi, 2017), we challenge hegemonic narratives and transform what learning could be toward justice. Facilitated process The symposium will be organized as a structured poster session, inviting participants to engage with various approaches to racial justice in the learning sciences and synthesize across a range of geographic, theoretical, and sociopolitical diversity. Our session will begin with initial framing by emerging researchers engaged with racial justice literature within and beyond the learning sciences. Each poster presenter will provide a brief overview of their work, then participants are invited to visit and engage more thoroughly with each of the eight posters at their own pace. Each poster will feature a raci al justice research design collaboration and respond to a series of questions rooted in racial justice theory and practice, including invitations to 1) Address the positioning of the community partnership and researcher(s), highlighting the role of relationality and identity in making specific knowledge production possible and productive, 2) Introduce the communities that the design collaborations are accountable to and describing the shared work in community, 3) Lay out the research questions and design goals, 4) Orient to particular traditions and lineages of racial justice theory and practice, and 5) Elaborate on how racial justice is prefigured through the communi ty design processes. Taken together, these posters demonstrate the diversity of racial justice work and bring a pedagogical stance to integrating racial justice scholarship into the learning sciences in theoretically grounded ways. We invite participants to engage the dialogue throughout the symposium. To this end, we will ask participants to consider: 1) As you engage with various explorations of racial justice research in this poster session, how are you conceptualizing racial justice in the learning sciences? 2) How might different conceptualizations of racial justice influence and impact your work and the communities you serve? 3) What questions do you have about racial justice research or how you might better facilitate racial justice in your own work? We will close with a synthesis of the overarching themes, offer insights on how we envision support within our field to foster 2382 meaningful and generative spaces for racial justice work and ignite discussion on what racial justice work might look like in participants’ research and design work. Working in good ways to prefigure abolition as racial justice Joe Curnow, Anny Chen Recently in Winnipeg, we have seen a proliferation of policing in everything from public libraries to grocery stores, justified through racialized language. We’ve seen similar “crime wave” discourses across North America, though in Winnipeg they have a distinctive anti -Indigenous framing (Wilt, 2024). However, a coalition of organizers have come together to fight for a city where investment in communities might create antiracist and anticolonial paths to community safety that do not rely on policing, prisons, and family separation. This coalition has struggled against mai nstream attitudes where safety means securitization and surveillance. How, then, do coalition organizers expand the imaginations of Winnipeggers beyond carceral solutions and design for abolitionist futures? The Abolitionist Futures Collective is a collective of prison and police abolitionist organizers in Winnipeg, MB, Canada. Our group includes people working on defunding police, prison rideshare, sex worker activists, library activists trying to remove secu rity screening from public libraries, Métis sovereignty groups, and others. We are a multiracial group with a plurality of non-binary/genderqueer folks. Joe (she/her) is a cis white woman with European and Latinx heritage. Anny (she/her) is a cis Canadian- born Chinese woman. Our research asks 1. How do we redefine safety toward community and away from colonial models of punishment, 2. How do we keep us safe, and 3. How do we facilitate politicization that enables participants in our workshops to imagine abolitionist futures? The Abolitionist Futures Collective works in Treaty 1 territory, the lands and waters of Nêhiyawak, Inninew, Anishinaabek, Oceti Sakowin Oyate, Michif, Anishininiiwak, and Denesuline people. This relationship calls on us to be in right relationship and attend to the ongoing colonial violence in Winnipeg. Racial justice is read through the long histories of Indigenous -led anticolonial resistance in Winnipeg (Sinclair, 2024), as well as Black feminist scholarship within prison and police abolition traditions (Dav is, 2011; Gilmore, 2007; Kaba, 2020). Racial justice shows up in our research design in two significant ways. First by drawing on lessons from Indigenous Elders, Knowledge Keepers, and community helpers, we have organized our work together through the Working in Good Ways framework (Ferland, Chen & Villagrán Becerra, n.d.). This approach offers resources for building strong relationships rooted in Indigenous ways of knowing and being while addressing historicized colonial power relations. Second, in our design we work to prefigure (Maeckelbergh, 2005; Curnow & Uttamchandani, 2022) abolitionist politics (Gilmore, 2007), where building relationships and community is a central outcome and process, where we plan for accessibility and attempt to integrate Dis ability Justice into our approach, where we strive to be in anti/decolonial relationship, and where we work to center racial justice. Getting real with racial justice: Lessons learned from technology spaces Stephanie T. Jones In this study, I focused on how Black computing practitioners understood the connections between Black Life and computing. I began with the theoretical perspective of Afrofuturism for thinking about potential visions for the future related to Black Life and Computing. However recurring refrains in the interviews were 1) the notion of what we can and should expect in a capitalist society, 2) the ways particular forms of Blackness are appreciated or denied, and 3) the ways historical events work as a guide for current decision making in the computing space. To describe the particular histories participants brought up, I offered the theoretical perspective of Plantation Prophecy, to discuss the ways the plantation is reified in society as a past, current, and “hopefully” future model for living globally. The early stages of this work were born out of a desire to more closely conduct analyses of how race and racialization shape the experience and design of learning environments. As an early career learning scientist, I struggled to find literature that talk ed about race and racism as shaping technology education. As a student of engineering and education in the US, I have been repeatedly impacted by the way the education system selects particular models of being as acceptable for those who are negatively racialized. During this time I also didn’t experience education on how race operates in engineering and education spaces - and thus had limited awareness of engineering as a political profession and as one where the work of race was to be a “good” minority (J ones & melo, 2021). In particular, this meant being under -aware of how my positionality as a Black femme was being shaped as a commodity for profit. 2383 In order to get real about racial justice, we have to get real about how race operates structurally and to consider where we would like to focus our energies if not racism (Bell, 1992). To do this, I integrate lessons from Black study (Morrison, 1987; Bell, 1992; Hartman, 2002; ross & Givens, 2023). I explore how Plantation Prophecy can be a useful analytical perspective for being racially literate when it comes to technology development. I think of racial justice not as a singular event but as an ongoing re -evaluation of commitments, relationships, and ways of knowing that take us away from subject/object relations. In this poster, I offer insights through Critical Discourse Analysis (Blommaert & Bulcaen, 2000; Ohito & Nyachae, 2019) of interviews to reveal ways Black computing practitioners were talking about racial justice and their potential role as a part of their work. Further,  I explore how practitioners became and are working to become racially literate given that these discussions rarely happen in computing. For example, overwhelmingly practitioners said “no” when asked if race had ever been discussed in computing classroom e nvironments - and how this lack of instruction led to moments of uncertainty in how to approach times of great contention, daily activities, and tokenization. Cross-cultural youth organizing and intergenerational learning Sarah Priscilla Lee How does intergenerational learning offer a generative framework for understanding how learning and teaching in a cross -cultural youth organizing group shows up and unfolds? How are relations across people and places situated within, shaped by, and engaged across sociopolitical, cultural, and historical realities on a municipal, national, and global scale (Tivaringe & Kirshner, 2021)? I look across two out-of-school settings: A youth summer program (ages 5–19) within a nonprofit refugee resettlement organization and Eternal Youth, a youth organizing group in a large midwestern city composed of Black, Latinx, South Asian, and Afghan refugee youth from middle school to college. In both spaces, participants represent a plethora of identities often reduced by labels like “youth” and "refugee." In Eternal Youth, I analyze how participants engage in meaning-making practices that resist hegemonic narratives and create liberatory possibilities on their terms. By examining how participants build relationships and structures by drawing on existing skills and experiences, I highlight how youth navigate transnational complexities and (re)shape the stories and relationships to each other and  to the spaces as woven across both spaces. Finally, in the design and facilitation of the summer program, we worked toward co- design to center students’ interests and support facilitator training rooted in care and culturally responsive practices (Ladson- Billings, 1995). This builds on the critical discourse around refugee education, focusing on the often-overlooked political subjectivities of refugee youth and families (Sukarieh & Tannock, 2014). At its core, this work examines the contradictions and possibilities of transnational identity and intergenerational learning toward building collective power and engaging education as a practice of freedom (hooks, 1994). Becoming racially literate as racial justice praxis Talia Leibovitz I conducted a four year ethnographic study analyzing a multi -racial group of middle-class parents organizing for racial justice in Oakland, California as a cis hetero white woman with eastern European  heritage who engages in anti-racist racial justice organizing in the K -12 education system. I utilize an interdisciplinary framework of critical policy analysis and socio-cultural theories of learning to consider how people learn and strategize toward racial justice amidst the local political economy they are organizing within. My research places education policy in conversation with the learning sciences, pushing the boundaries of both disciplines to demonstrate that education policy scholars and scholars of learning must understand how and what policy actors learned about education policy and racial justice. Much of the existing research on middle -class parents across racial groups organizing for racial justice in education illustrates how despite the best of intentions (Lewis & Diamond, 2015), these parents often reproduce the very inequalities they aim to ameliorate. Building from this research, I consider how middle -class parents across racial groups engage in moment-to-moment interactions that shape their learning for racial justice in ways that afford a rearticulation of racialized ideologies. I draw from Stuart Hall’s understanding that ideologies are constantly contested and at times, transformed (Hall, 1996). Societal transformat ion occurs via rearticulation where ideological connections are disrupted, and new ones are created (Hall, 1996). Hall’s framing of articulation is particularly relevant given this study’s focus on how a group of parents came to contest commonly held racialized ideologies of school quality in ways that not only shaped their learning of racialization but also their organizing strategies for racial justice. I also orient to racial justice through Scott and Bajaj’s (2022) use of racialization to analytically consider how people or groups come to be classified beyond identity, and how these 2384 categories are connected to political, social, and economic dynamics that have consequences for people’s life opportunities. I developed an original conceptual framework that integrated theories of political economy and socio- cultural approaches to learning in order to capture the macro conditions that shape inequality in an urban district, while also documenting and learning from the moment-to-moment interactions through which people make sense of inequality and organize toward racial justice. This interdisciplinary framework allowed me to ask how the socio-political context of a school district informs the discourse and policies of educational efforts and how people learn about racial equity through their organizing. The design of my study as an ethnographic case study allowed me to analyze learning over time as organizers for racial justice responded to political events that unfolded in the school district. The multiple years of observations were a critical design of my study given that racial literacy is not a location one arrives at but rather a process that occurs over time in a non-linear way, This contributed to a rich analysis of how people collectively became racially literate through their  organizing and how their collective racial literacy informed new organizing strategies to respond to the political economy of the school district. “We be knowing”: Uplifting black women’s knowledge toward justice Nicollette D. Mitchell My research, through the Black Women in Geoscience Education project, centers Black women in the United States who have earned post -secondary degree(s) in geosciences. I currently seek our (Black -woman- geoscientists) own ontological, epistemological, and methodological ways of conceiving disciplinary learning as a form of racial justice. Such positioning is made necessary because the geosciences, which has been imperative in describing Earth’s systems and processes, has remained the least demographically diverse of all science, engineering, mathematics, and technology fields (Bernard and Cooperdock, 2018). To elevate the experiences of Black women in this context, I have adopted an intersectional frame (Crenshaw 1991) to consider  structural, political, and representational aspects of Black women’s geoscience experiences. This structural, political, and representational approach to research helps to further elucidate forms of thriving in a racialized -gendered space that has historically positioned Black women in a deficit- oriented way. My goal through this work is to engage in  Black feminist praxis – and interweaving of theory, practice, and methods -  which empowers Black women through the disruption of oppressive ideas and practices (Porter and colleagues, 2023). I am a Black woman immigrant mother, scholar, and former paleoclimatologist who is currently enrolled in a doctoral program within the learning sciences. I approach racial justice from a Black feminist ontological space (Collins, 2022), which urges me to believe in the liberatory capacity of learning. Said otherwise, teaching and learning have always been important to me, my mothers, aunties, and sisters and will always be. I cannot divorce my understanding of how and what is learned from that inheritance. I find myself here in community with other scholars who conceive of learning and racial justice as interrelated formations. This exercise, of th inking through and articulating what racial justice means in learning sciences, gives me hope. In conceiving of what racial justice means in the context of my scholarly contributions to learning science, it is imperative that the work acknowledges and explores (for me, participants, and the reader) both/and (Collins, 2022) – the nuances of being simultaneously marginalized and agentic.   Within the context of the Black Women  in Geoscience Education Project, that means that the research design, analysis, and discussion centers are responsive to the needs of Black women. Creating space for Black women to speak to their/our own experiences as knowledgeable is a part of disrupting epistemic injustice about what counts as disciplinary learning. In pursuit of justice, then, I work to amplify that which is already known in ways that refute colonial logics that requi re extraction from multiply marginalized people for the use of the academy. Prototyping black speculative justice learning among future educators at a PWI Ashieda McKoy With an increasing number of students of color in schools and a largely white teaching population, we in the learning sciences (have and still) need to be thinking about how we study and design more inclusive and justice - centered learning environments for our young people and their future educators (NASEM, 2024). Here, I believe that Afrofuturism as an aesthetic, pedagogy, and sensibility for design, offers a critically innovative lens to study and craft justice-centered learning for all educators. I point to a Black speculative, namely Afrofuturist, orientation of racial justice that situates justice work in exploring how race and diverse cultural experiences affect pedagogical 2385 reality, knowledge, design, and (learning) futures (Cann, 2016; Womack, 2013) and, more importantly how, in community with each other, we can and should (re)imagine and (re)invent the alternative technologies, realities and futures of our Black freedom dreams (Carey, 2020; Faison and McArthur, 2020; Love, 2019). Noting this largely white femme educator population, my project especially involves making sure that white educators realize they are important and necessary factors in concretizing the just (learning) futures we need. This study takes place in an emerging educator course at a primarily white institution (PWI) whose educators go on to serve largely urban Black and Latinx students. I ask: How can future educator environments be designed to support the development of pedagogical theories and practices oriented toward just Black futures? For this dissertation project, I redesigned a teacher learning ecology using Afrofuturist principles of learning and design and sociocultural theories of learning. Primarily organized around four main Afrofuturist learning guides–justice-centered, future-oriented, technology-mediated, and collective, my course design supports future educators in grappling and experimenting with new pedagogical theories and practices for more just learning futures that are developed in iteration with youth, are justice -centered and tech-mediated. As such, this course and dissertation study is specifically designed to center the theories and practices of Black, Brown, and Queer thinkers, educators, and youth, to understand justice -centered learning through cycles of iterative design where future educators and youth “prototype” new ideas and theories for more liberatory futures. Ultimately, the (re)design of this course offe rs new windows into the design of a justice -centered teacher learning environment that is offered within the context of PWI university-based teacher education. Latina testimonios of failure: Trenzas of failure, learning, and survivance in the Latina experience Beatriz Salazar Over the last 20 years in the field of learning sciences, there has been an increasing amount of research surrounding failure and the experiences of failure as opportunities for learning. However, what has often been left out of the conversation, until more recently, has been the ways identity impacts the ways learners experience failure. In the United States, girls and young women of color often receive negative consequences as a result of asking questions in the classroom (Annamma et al, 2019). Instead, perfection and a lack of questions are rewarded in the education system, despite the research supporting opportunities for failure, mistakes , and questions (Kapur, 2008; McNamara, 2001; Van Lehn et al., 2003). Guided by the framework of trenzas and greñas (Montoya, 1994) and implementing testimonio (Delgado-Bernal, 1998) as a method, this dissertation explores how Latinas in the United States experience self - identified failures and the learning that stems from these experiences. Much like Montoya’s experience in trenzas and greñas, Latinas and people of color, wear masks that hide our greñas, our imperfections in our braided lives. This is a notion that is especially true for those who are children of immigrants,  who often believe that failure is not an option after their parents gave up so much for them (Romano, 2022). Together, the researcher and the collaborators learn how to explore this racial justice issue through a collaborative, decolonized methodology. Without these masks, our true and whole selves might not be accepted by others. This work seeks to challenge the notion that to be imperfect means you are a failure. Without mistakes and the room to self -reflect, process, and re -mediate our errors in true vulnerability, people of color are robbed of the opportunity to learn, while the system is robbed of the opportunity to acknowledge its wrongs. As a Latina daughter of immigrant parents growing up in the US, I challenge the notion that “failure is not an option” or that to fail means to become a failure that youth of color and children of immigrants carry. We are not perfect, nor are we meant to be. We too deserve the opportunity to learn and grow. Facilitating learning with data for racial justice Trang C. Tran, Joseph L. Polman, Katherine Miller, Raesheena Kennedy, Rachel Folger We are a group of interdisciplinary education researchers and classroom educators, from a project named DataPBL. In our codesign effort, two teachers (Kennedy & Folger) engaged with data specialists, curriculum developers, and learning scientists to build data-focused addendums, including curating and customizing datasets, for existing curricula that blend Social Studies and ELA content. Our work serves students who are attending Marbles Expeditionary, a charter K -8 school located in the midwest U.S. serving predominantly Black low - and middle-income students, and Oak Park Expeditionary, a public K -12 school located in the northeastern U.S., serving predominantly Latine American students, and students from immigrant families. Across their middle school classrooms, we observed how  instructors introduced and scaffolded data practices that were grounded in 2386 and entwined with their commitment to promote racial equity and racial justice. We co -developed an interest in exploring the sociopolitical implications of teaching, learning, and creating with data. Specifically, how may classroom educators facilitate learning with data for racial justice? Our approach to racial justice issue focused on 1) constructing high -quality curricula that center and serve our own students to unsettle a normalized reality in which Black and Brown youth are seldomly prioritized in learning materials (Dumas, 2014; McKinney de Royston et al., 2021) and 2) interrogating and counteracting the systemic neglect of Japanese American injustice and Asian Americans across K -20 curricula (An, 2016). We describe two teachers' adaptations and enactments of a curriculum module that examines the mass incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II. In Folger’s class, students studied the history of immigration to the US in the 20th century, the role immigration and citizenship played in the experience of Japanese incarceration, and current trends in migration and detention, engaging multiple datasets to explore the question “Who gets to be an American?” Kennedy’s data lessons delved into “sense of belonging” as an enduring dilemma affecting generations of immigrants and racially marginalized communities. Students worked with datasets to unveil the stories of Japanese American prisoners before, during, an d after incarceration and the current -day experience of refugees in students’ local state; furthermore, students collected their own data embracing the sense of belonging at their own school community. In this poster, we examine the range of activities and interactions with data that our classroom educators and their students employed to challenge systemic violence and deficit narratives on the Japanese and Asian American communities. We explore the role that youth's intersectional identities played in their emotional responses and perspective -taking regarding various racial injustices, including those affecting immigrant, refugee communities, and their own racialized school communities. papers.title: Small vs. Large Language Models: Comparing Language Models in Generating Productive Failure Math Problems
papers.authors: Seyedahmad Rahimi, Salah Esmaeiligoujar, Deniz Ercan, Maryam Babaee, Ran Gao
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT -4o can generate high -quality math problems but are resource -intensive and difficult to fine -tune. Small language models (SLMs) like Phi-3 may provide a more practical alternative, as they can run locally and be adapted for specific tasks. In this study, we generated 60 Productive Failure (PF) math problems, with half produced by GPT-4o and half by Phi-3. To ensure comparability, we controlled for grade level, Common Core standard, theme, interest, and prior knowledge. Trained raters evaluated the problems across five PF dimensions. Results showed that GPT -4o ( M = 13.38; SD  = 1.88) outperformed Phi-3 (M = 10.67; SD = 2.73), with a large effect size ( d = 1.16). These findings indicate that although GPT -4o currently generates more effective PF problems, Phi -3 shows promising potential. With further fine-tuning and task-specific adaptation, SLMs like Phi-3 may offer a sustainable, cost-effective solution for educational problem generation.
